- Overview of legislation impacting pharmacy network access: Medicare Part D and many state laws limit the Company’s and client health plans’ ability to restrict pharmacy networks or remove providers; “any willing provider” requirements; state limits on pharmacy audits that hinder recovery of overpayments; restrictions on special benefit structures favoring affiliated pharmacies, potentially reducing client and consumer savings.
- Pharmacy pricing regulation: State laws governing PBMs’ use of Maximum Allowable Cost (MAC) for generics, including disclosure, eligible drug types, and pharmacy appeal rights; restrictions on retroactive reconciliations/recoupments; possible mandates to use reimbursement benchmarks like NADAC or WAC plus a dispensing fee, which could impede cost management.
- Formulary and plan design controls: Federal oversight by HHS/CMS of Medicare Part D formularies and ACA essential health benefits; influence of NAIC, NCQA, and URAC standards; state rules on drug coverage and delivery channels; prohibitions on certain benefit designs (limited networks, mandated provider use, copay differentials, formulary tiering) that may constrain formulary and network strategies.
- Retail/LTC segment regulations: State rules for retail medical clinics (physician oversight, licensing, corporate practice of medicine limits, signage, contracting, facilities, scope of services) that may affect operations and expansion.
- Additional retail operational laws: Restrictions on alcohol sales, minimum wage mandates, regulations governing optometry and audiology practices, dietician services, and sales of durable medical equipment, contact lenses, eyeglasses, and hearing aids.
- Corporate information: CVS Health Corporation incorporated in Delaware (1996), headquarters in Woonsocket, RI, listed on NYSE under “CVS,” with general company information available to the public.

structure.heading: Item 1A: Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase: You should carefully consider each of the following risks and uncertainties and all of the other information set forth in this 10-K.
structure.summary:
- How CVS Health communicates investor information: availability of SEC filings and press releases on its website; use of the investor site and @CVSHealthIR per Regulation FD; SEC site reference; website content not incorporated into the 10-K.
- Item 1A. Risk Factors (summary and detail):
  - Business risks: ongoing and uncertain impacts of COVID-19; difficulty forecasting health care and benefit costs; adverse macroeconomic conditions (inflation, interest rates, supply chains); intense competition across Health Care Benefits, PBM, and Retail/LTC; shifts in product mix (insured vs. ASC, growth in government programs); challenges competing profitably on Public Exchanges; negative public perception of the industry; dependence on maintaining customer relationships and demand, including proprietary brands; drug availability, pricing, and safety; actuarial/reserving uncertainty; exposure to other insurers’ solvency; extreme events and disasters; and ability to meet ESG goals.
  - Legal/regulatory and public policy risks: potential changes to U.S. health care system (ACA, Medicare, Medicaid), drug pricing and PBM regulation; complex compliance obligations and potential penalties; exposure to false claims, anti-kickback, ERISA, and privacy/security laws; frequent audits, investigations, and reviews (DOJ/CMS/OIG), including risk adjustment scrutiny and RADV; evolving litigation profile as offerings expand; Medicare/Medicaid-specific issues (rate setting, star ratings, coverage decisions, service area expansion, encounter data accuracy, redeterminations, pharmacy performance program changes, Part D funding and rules); reliance on government-funded programs and budget/funding risks; changes to pricing benchmarks (AWP/WAC/NADAC/AAC) and potential congressional action; constraints on premium rate approvals and minimum MLR requirements; employer-related labor law changes; and heightened international compliance, data protection, anti-corruption, and geopolitical risks.
  - Mergers, acquisitions, alliances, and divestitures: integration complexity and execution risk; continued pursuit of inorganic growth (including Oak Street Health and Signify Health), regulatory approvals, potential liabilities, dilution, added debt, and termination fee exposure; goodwill/intangible valuation risks; joint venture governance and compliance challenges; and divestiture execution risks.
  - Operational and technology risks: meeting customer and member service expectations; persistent cybersecurity threats and incidents (including vendor-related) and data governance/privacy compliance; IT system failures, modernization complexity, vendor dependencies; payment processing, fraud, and network rule compliance; business continuity hazards (natural disasters, unrest, supply/distribution disruptions); talent attraction/retention and succession planning; sales channel reliance on internal teams and third‑party brokers/agents and related marketing compliance; and need for effective collaboration across business units.
  - Financial and market risks: capital deployment effectiveness and potential impacts of credit rating changes; impairment risks for goodwill and intangibles; volatility in capital markets and interest rates affecting investment portfolio values, income, liquidity, and counterparties.
  - Relationships with manufacturers, providers, suppliers, and vendors: dependence on drug manufacturers/suppliers (including limited sources and imports), supply shortages, pricing pressure on generics and brands; provider network contracting and value-based arrangements; vendor compliance failures leading to regulatory, legal, or reputational harm; disputes and higher costs from out‑of‑network providers; and provider consolidation increasing costs and competition.
- Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments: none.
- Item 2. Properties: description of principal offices and facilities by segment, including headquarters in Woonsocket, RI, and Hartford, CT; PBM pharmacies and sites; Retail/LTC footprint (store count, clinics, distribution centers, LTC pharmacies) and legacy lease guarantees.

structure.start_phrase:
The following discussion and analysis should be read in conjunction with the audited consolidated financial statements and related notes included in Item 8 of
this Annual Report on Form 10-K (this “10-K”), “Risk Factors” included in Item 1A of this 10-K and the “Cautionary Statement Concerning Forward-
Looking Statements” in this 10-K.
structure.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Management’s Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) for CVS Health’s 10-K, to be read with audited financials, Risk Factors, and forward-looking statements.
- Company overview: Integrated health solutions company with retail pharmacies, MinuteClinic, PBM, specialty and senior pharmacy care, and health insurance offerings. Four reportable segments: Health Care Benefits (HCB), Pharmacy Services (PBM), Retail/LTC, and Corporate/Other.
- Segment overviews:
  - Health Care Benefits: Broad Insured and ASC health products (medical, pharmacy, dental, behavioral), Medicare Advantage/Supplement, PDP, Medicaid; entry into ACA public exchanges in additional states in 2022–2023; diverse customer base.
  - Pharmacy Services: Full PBM suite (plan design, formulary, network, mail, specialty/infusion, medical spend mgmt), 340B administration, GPO manufacturer contracting, and pharma services; diverse plan sponsor clients; multiple dispensing channels.
  - Retail/LTC: Retail pharmacies, MinuteClinic services, diagnostics, vaccinations (flu, COVID-19, shingles), long-term care pharmacy operations; significant U.S. retail Rx market share; large physical and digital footprint.
  - Corporate/Other: Enterprise management/admin costs, transformation and modernization investments, acquisition integration, and runoff products (e.g., large case pensions, long-term care insurance).
- COVID-19 impacts (2020–2022):
  - HCB: Sharp utilization decline in 2020 then normalization; 2021 volatility from variants; 2022 stabilization as pricing captured COVID costs; membership mix shifts (Commercial declines, Medicaid increases in 2020).
  - Retail/LTC: Initial 2020 surge in prescriptions and front store, then traffic declines; large-scale testing and vaccinations through 2021–2022; 2022 saw fewer vaccinations/diagnostic tests but strong OTC test kit demand; uncertainty persists.
- Consolidated 2022 vs. 2021 results:
  - Revenues up 10.4% to $322.5B, driven by growth across all segments.
  - Operating income down 41.3% to $7.7B due to $5.8B opioid litigation charges and $2.5B loss on assets held for sale (Omnicare LTC write-down); offset by absence of 2021 store/goodwill impairments and gains on bswift and PayFlex sales.
  - Operating expenses up 3.1% (support growth, investments, lower legal settlement gains), but decreased as % of revenue (11.8%).
  - Interest expense declined with lower debt; effective tax rate rose to 26.0% (nondeductible legal charges, divestiture basis differences).
- 2023 outlook:
  - HCB: Medicare and Commercial membership growth; Medicaid declines from redeterminations.
  - PBM: Purchasing economics improvements and strong network volume; offset by client price improvements and pricing regulation.
  - Retail/LTC: Higher prescription volume and improved generic purchasing; offset by reimbursement pressure and lower COVID-related contributions.
  - Enterprise cost savings from digital/tech/analytics, workforce/workplace strategies, and vendor/procurement initiatives; continued regulatory and COVID-related uncertainty.
- Segment performance (highlights, 2022 vs. 2021):
  - Health Care Benefits: Revenues +11.2%; MBR improved to 84.0% (favorable COVID net); gains on bswift/PayFlex; adjusted operating income +19.4%. Medical membership up to 24.4M; Medicare star ratings mix declined (21% ≥4 stars for 2023 vs. 87% prior year basis). Small loss on assets held for sale (Thailand).
  - Pharmacy Services: Revenues +10.6% on higher claims, specialty growth, brand inflation; adjusted operating income +7.2% on improved purchasing economics (GPO), partially offset by client price improvements; total claims +4.1%; generic dispensing rate up to 87.4%.
  - Retail/LTC: Revenues +6.5% (Rx and front store volume, cough/cold/flu, OTC test kits); adjusted operating income −12.0% (lower COVID vaccinations/testing, reimbursement pressure, higher investments); $2.5B loss on LTC assets held for sale; 2021 store and goodwill impairments absent in 2022; same-store sales: pharmacy +9.5%, front store +7.4%; prescriptions filled +2.3%; GDR 87.4%.
  - Corporate/Other: Revenues −26.5% (net realized capital losses, lower PE income); $5.8B opioid litigation charges; higher adjusted operating loss (lower investment income, LTC insurance reserve strengthening).
- Liquidity and capital resources:
  - Strong liquidity; 12/31/22 cash and equivalents ~$12.9B; operating cash flow down to $16.2B (timing, inventory).
  - Investing: lower net investment purchases; proceeds from bswift/PayFlex; capex ~$2.7B (majority to tech/digital/strategic).
  - Financing: less cash used (lower debt repayments), share repurchases in 2022; store count reduced (closures).
  - No commercial paper outstanding; ample undrawn backup credit facilities; FHLB capacity unused.
  - 2022 redemptions of near-term notes; prior years’ debt tenders and one 2021 issuance; derivative use for hedging.
  - Investment-grade ratings (Moody’s Baa2, S&P BBB, stable outlooks).
  - Share repurchases: $10B authorizations in 2021 and 2022; 2022 buybacks ~$3.5B; ASRs executed in 2022 and early 2023.
  - Dividends: quarterly increased 10% to $0.605 in 2023.
  - Future cash obligations detailed (leases, debt, interest, opioid settlements, insurance liabilities).
  - Regulatory dividend constraints at subs; adequate RBC across insurance/HMO subsidiaries.
- Critical accounting policies and estimates:
  - Revenue recognition across segments, including Medicare Part D risk corridors, PBM gross presentation with retail co-pays, rebates/guarantees, loyalty programs (ExtraCare, CarePass), LTC variable consideration.
  - Securities impairment (credit vs. yield-related); vendor allowances/purchase discounts; inventory valuation and shrink reserves.
  - Leases and right-of-use assets; long-lived asset recoverability (2022 office real estate optimization charges $117M; 2021 $1.4B retail store impairments).
  - Goodwill testing (no 2022 impairment; 2021 LTC impairment $431M; Commercial Business sensitivity).
  - Health care costs payable/IBNR methodologies and sensitivities; income tax uncertainties and valuation.
- Market risk disclosures:
  - Interest rate, credit quality, market valuation, FX, commodity, and operational risks; derivative use limited to hedging.
  - Investment portfolio composition, credit quality (average A), fair value levels, and impairment approach; experience-rated product differentiation.

structure.title: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.heading: Item 7A: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.start_phrase:
The Company’s earnings and financial condition are exposed to interest rate risk, credit quality risk, market valuation risk, foreign currency risk, commodity
risk and operational risk.
structure.summary:
- Covers Item 7A: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk, detailing exposures to interest rate, credit quality, market valuation, foreign currency, commodity, and operational risks, plus Item 8 index to financial statements.
- Interest rate and credit quality risk management: duration matching of assets/liabilities, high average credit quality and sector diversification; derivatives used primarily for hedging (interest rate swaps, treasury rate locks, forwards, futures, warrants, put options, credit default swaps).
- Investments (as of Dec 31): total portfolio $23.9B in 2022 ($26.1B in 2021), supporting experience-rated products $0.7B ($1.0B) and remaining products $23.1B ($25.2B). Experience-rated product risks largely borne by contract holders; assets may be withdrawable.
- Credit quality: average rating A in 2022 and 2021; AAA fair value ~$6.0B (2022) and $6.7B (2021). Below-investment-grade debt $1.9B (2022) and $2.3B (2021), of which 1.6% and 2.0% support experience-rated products. Municipal securities guaranteed by third parties $202M (2022) and $305M (2021), ~1% of total; AA+/AA with guarantees; A without; no significant guarantor concentration.
- Valuation and impairment: debt securities generally classified as available for sale and carried at fair value; <1% valued with Level 3 inputs. Impairment policy: if intent/requirement to sell, write down to fair value through income; otherwise bifurcate into credit-related allowance through income and non-credit-related component in OCI. Impairment of debt securities is a critical accounting policy.
- Market valuation risk analysis: quarterly sensitivity reviews. Scenario at 12/31/22 assumes +100 bps interest rates and -15% publicly traded domestic equity prices.
  - +100 bps: long-term debt fair value decline ~$2.9B ($3.6B pretax), not affecting operating results/financial condition; net decline ~$595M ($750M pretax) for interest-sensitive investments/liabilities tied to continuing non-experience-rated products (recognized as unrealized loss in equity).
  - -15% equities: net decline ~$20M ($26M pretax).
  - Conclusion: changes would not materially affect near-term consolidated financial condition, results, or cash flows.
- Foreign currency and commodity risk: no material derivative positions; exposure not material at 12/31/22 and 12/31/21.
- Operational risks: COVID-19-related operational impacts (facility closures, labor shortages, supply/distribution/infrastructure disruptions); remote work increases IT demand and cyber risks (phishing, malware, account takeovers, DDoS, scanning). Company and vendors have experienced varied attacks; significant ongoing investment in cybersecurity; no material impact through 12/31/22; Board and relevant committees regularly briefed.
- Item 8 index: consolidated statements of operations, comprehensive income, balance sheets, cash flows, shareholders’ equity for 2020–2022; notes to consolidated financial statements; and auditor reports (PCAOB ID: 42) with page references.

structure.title: Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
structure.heading: Item 8: Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
structure.start_phrase: See accompanying notes to consolidated financial statements.
structure.summary:
- Scope and structure: Item 8 – Financial Statements and Supplementary Data, including consolidated statements (Operations, Comprehensive Income, Balance Sheets, Cash Flows, Shareholders’ Equity), Notes, and the Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm’s report (PCAOB ID: 42).

- Performance (Consolidated Statements of Operations, 2022–2020):
  - Total revenues grew from $268.7B (2020) to $292.1B (2021) to $322.5B (2022), driven by products ($226.6B in 2022), premiums ($85.3B), and services.
  - 2022 included significant charges: $5.8B opioid litigation and $2.5B loss on assets held for sale; 2021 included $1.4B store impairments and $0.4B goodwill impairment.
  - Operating income declined to $7.7B (2022) from $13.2B (2021); net income attributable to CVS Health fell to $4.1B (2022) from $7.9B (2021).
  - Diluted EPS: $3.14 (2022), $5.95 (2021), $5.46 (2020). Dividends per share: $2.20 (2022) vs. $2.00 (2021, 2020).

- Comprehensive income:
  - 2022 comprehensive income attributable to CVS Health dropped to $1.7B, primarily due to negative other comprehensive income driven by net unrealized investment losses ($2.3B).

- Financial position (Balance Sheets at Dec 31):
  - Total assets decreased to $228.3B (2022) from $233.0B (2021); cash and cash equivalents rose to $12.9B; assets held for sale of $0.9B appeared in 2022.
  - Total liabilities modestly decreased to $157.0B; long-term debt ~$50.5B.
  - Shareholders’ equity declined to $71.3B, with AOCI swinging from +$1.0B (2021) to -$1.5B (2022) and higher treasury stock reflecting repurchases.

- Cash flows (2022–2020):
  - Strong operating cash flow: $16.2B (2022), $18.3B (2021), $15.9B (2020).
  - Investing cash use of $5.0B in 2022 (notably property and equipment purchases); financing cash use of $10.5B (debt repayments, $3.5B share repurchases, $2.9B dividends).
  - Ending cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash: $13.3B (2022).

- Shareholders’ equity changes:
  - Activities include stock-based compensation, ESPP, treasury share purchases (net $3.7B in 2022), dividends, and OCI movements.
  - Note of ASU 2016-13 adoption in 2020 with a minor retained earnings adjustment.

- Business overview and accounting policies:
  - Description of CVS Health’s integrated model: retail pharmacies/clinics, PBM, specialty pharmacy, senior pharmacy care, and health insurance offerings (including Medicare Advantage and Part D).
  - Four reportable segments: Health Care Benefits, Pharmacy Services, Retail/LTC, and Corporate/Other.
  - Segment highlights:
    - Health Care Benefits: broad insured and ASC offerings; entry into Public Exchanges in eight states in 2022, four more in 2023.
    - Pharmacy Services: comprehensive PBM solutions, specialty, infusion, GPO, and 340B services.
    - Retail/LTC: prescriptions, health/wellness products, MinuteClinic services, diagnostics, vaccinations, and long-term care pharmacy.
  - Note on ongoing COVID-19 impacts across operations.

For 2022, total revenues were $322.5B (products $226.6B, premiums $85.3B, services $9.7B), with operating costs reflecting $5.8B opioid litigation charges and a $2.5B loss on assets held for sale (2021 included $1.4B store impairments and $0.4B goodwill impairment). nodes.start_phrase: CVS Health Corporation, together with its subsidiaries (collectively, “CVS Health” or the “Company”), has more than 9,000 retail locations, more than 1,100 walk-in medical clinics,
nodes.summary:
- This excerpt is from the Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements (Significant Accounting Policies – Description of Business) for CVS Health Corporation.
- It outlines CVS Health’s integrated health care model and scale: 9,000+ retail locations, 1,100+ walk-in clinics (MinuteClinic), a leading PBM with 110M+ plan members, specialty pharmacy solutions, senior pharmacy care, and health insurance offerings serving ~35M people (including Medicare Advantage and a leading standalone Medicare Part D plan).
- The Company asserts its integrated model improves access, outcomes, and costs.
- It notes COVID-19’s continuing impact on operations, results, cash flows, and financial condition for 2020–2022, with references to broader 10-K discussion.
- CVS Health has four reportable segments: Health Care Benefits, Pharmacy Services, Retail/LTC, and Corporate/Other.
- Health Care Benefits segment: a diversified health benefits provider offering medical, pharmacy, dental, behavioral health, medical management, Medicare Advantage, Medicare Supplement, PDPs, Medicaid management, and health IT services. Customers include employers, individuals (including Public Exchange participants), students, part-time/hourly workers, health plans, providers, governments, labor groups, and expatriates. It distinguishes Insured vs. administrative services contract (ASC) products. Entered individual Public Exchanges in eight states in Jan 2022 and four more in Jan 2023. Previously provided workers’ compensation administrative services until a July 31, 2020 divestiture.
- Pharmacy Services segment: provides comprehensive PBM solutions (plan design, formulary, retail network management, mail order), specialty pharmacy and infusion, clinical and disease management, medical spend management, and services for providers and 340B Covered Entities. Operates a group purchasing organization negotiating drug pricing and rebates, and offers administrative/management/reporting services to pharmaceutical manufacturers. Clients include employers, insurers, unions, government groups, health plans, PDPs, Medicaid managed care plans, Public and private exchange plans, and Covered Entities. Operates specialty retail and mail pharmacies, mail dispensing, compounding pharmacies, and infusion/enteral nutrition branches.
- Retail/LTC segment: sells prescription drugs and a broad range of health/wellness and general merchandise, delivers care via MinuteClinic, provides diagnostic testing and vaccinations (e.g., influenza, COVID-19, shingles), and runs long-term care pharmacy operations that dispense medications and provide consulting and ancillary services (description truncated).

- Restricted cash: Current—funds held on behalf of members (including HSA funds) reported in other current assets; Noncurrent—amounts held in a captive insurance trust to satisfy collateral for certain assigned insurance policies, reported in other assets; invested in time deposits and money market funds.
- Cash reconciliation (2020–2022): Total cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash of $13,305M (2022), $12,691M (2021), $11,043M (2020); 2022 components include cash and cash equivalents $12,945M, restricted cash current $144M, restricted cash noncurrent $216M.
- Notable change: 2022 decrease in restricted cash within other current assets primarily due to lower HSA funds following the sale of PayFlex.

nodes.title: Restricted Cash
nodes.heading: 1.9 Restricted Cash
nodes.start_phrase: Restricted cash included in other current assets on the consolidated balance sheets represents funds held on behalf of members, including health savings account (“HSA”) funds associated with high deductible health plans.
nodes.summary:
- Describes CVS Health’s Retail/LTC segment footprint as of December 31, 2022: more than 9,000 retail locations, over 1,100 MinuteClinic sites, online retail pharmacy, long-term care (LTC) pharmacies, and on-site pharmacies.
- Outlines the Corporate/Other segment, which includes enterprise-wide management and administrative functions (executive management, corporate relations, legal, compliance, HR, IT, finance), transformation and modernization investments, acquisition integration costs, and runoff products no longer sold (large case pensions and long-term care insurance).
- States the basis of presentation: consolidated financial statements prepared under U.S. GAAP, including majority-owned subsidiaries and VIEs where CVS Health is the primary beneficiary; all material intercompany balances and transactions eliminated.
- Notes use of estimates impacting reported amounts, with potential differences from actual results.
- Defines cash and cash equivalents (maturities of three months or less; includes highly liquid money market funds, commercial paper, time deposits, and certain other debt securities).
- Explains restricted cash: current (funds held on behalf of members, including HSA funds) and noncurrent (trust funds in a captive insurer for collateral), invested in time deposits and money market funds. Provides cash reconciliation totals: 2022—$13,305 million; 2021—$12,691 million; 2020—$11,043 million. Highlights the 2022 decrease in current restricted cash due to the PayFlex sale.
- Details investment accounting:
  - Debt securities (U.S. Treasury/agency, MBS, corporate/foreign bonds) classified as available-for-sale at fair value; current or long-term based on maturity/intent. Impairment model distinguishes intent-to-sell write-downs through earnings versus credit-related allowances (through earnings) and non-credit losses (OCI) when not intending or required to sell. Interest accrual ceases when collection is unlikely. For MBS/ABS, income recognized using effective yield with adjustments for updated prepayment estimates through earnings.
  - Equity securities measured at fair value with changes recognized in net income.
- Covers mortgage loans measured at unpaid principal less allowance for credit losses; current if due or committed to prepay within 12 months. Loans are pooled by similar risk characteristics (LTV, property type, geography, vacancy, condition). Credit loss reserves use a loss-rate method incorporating expected severity and default probability, adjusted for reasonable and supportable macroeconomic forecasts (e.g., GDP, employment) with reversion to historical loss rates thereafter. Interest on potential problem or restructured loans is accrued if collectible and performing; for problem loans (e.g., >60 days delinquent, bankruptcy, foreclosure), interest is on a cash basis, and foreclosure-period cash receipts reduce principal.

nodes.title: Debt Securities
nodes.heading: 1.10 Debt Securities
nodes.start_phrase: Debt securities consist primarily of U.S. Treasury and agency securities, mortgage-backed securities, corporate and foreign bonds and other debt securities.
nodes.summary:
- Defines investment categories: debt securities (U.S. Treasury/agency, mortgage-backed, corporate/foreign, other), equity securities, and mortgage loans.
- Classification: investments designated as current or long-term based on contractual maturity unless intended to be sold within 12 months; debt securities classified as available-for-sale and carried at fair value; equity securities with readily available fair values measured at fair value with changes in net income; mortgage loans carried at unpaid principal balance net of an allowance.
- Debt securities impairment: if intent or requirement to sell before recovery, write down to fair value with loss in net income; otherwise bifurcate unrealized losses into credit-related (recognized in net income via an allowance, limited to fair value shortfall) and non-credit-related (recognized in OCI). Assessment considers price decline magnitude, issuer/industry/geography conditions, security payment structure, payment delinquencies, and rating changes. Interest is not accrued when collection is unlikely.
- Credit-related loss measurement: compare present value of expected cash flows to amortized cost; record allowance for the shortfall, capped by the difference between amortized cost and fair value.
- Mortgage- and asset-backed securities income recognition: use effective yield based on anticipated prepayments and economic life; adjust yield retrospectively for changes in prepayment estimates with impacts recorded in net income.
- Mortgage loans: classify as current if maturity or committed prepayment is within 12 months; group loans into risk pools with similar characteristics (e.g., LTV, property type, geography, vacancy, condition) for expected credit loss measurement.
- Mortgage loan credit losses: apply a loss-rate method using expected loss severity and default probability; incorporate reasonable and supportable economic forecasts (e.g., GDP, employment) and revert to historical loss rates beyond the forecast period.
- Mortgage loan interest recognition: accrue on potential problem or restructured loans to the extent collectible and performing; recognize on a cash basis for problem loans (e.g., >60 days delinquent, bankruptcy, foreclosure); treat cash received during foreclosure as principal return.

nodes.title: Equity Securities
nodes.heading: 1.11 Equity Securities
nodes.start_phrase: Equity securities with readily available fair values are measured at fair value with changes in fair value recognized in net income.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Company’s accounting policies for investments, covering debt securities, equity securities, and mortgage loans.
- Debt securities:
  - Types include U.S. Treasury/agency, mortgage-backed, corporate, foreign, and other debt.
  - Classified as current or long-term based on contractual maturity unless intended to be sold within 12 months (then current).
  - Classified as available-for-sale and measured at fair value (see Note 4 for valuation).
  - Impairment:
    - If intent or requirement to sell before recovery: write down to fair value with loss in net income.
    - If not selling: bifurcate loss into credit-related (recognized via allowance for credit losses in net income) and non-credit-related (recognized in other comprehensive income).
    - Credit assessment considers fair value vs amortized cost, issuer/industry/geography conditions, payment structure, missed payments, and rating changes.
    - Credit loss amount based on PV of expected cash flows vs amortized cost, limited to the fair value shortfall.
  - Nonaccrual: stop accruing interest when collection is unlikely.
  - MBS/ABS income recognition: effective yield method using anticipated prepayments; yield and carrying amount adjusted retrospectively with impacts to net income.
- Equity securities:
  - Measured at fair value with changes recognized in net income.
- Mortgage loans:
  - Carried at unpaid principal balance net of an allowance for credit losses.
  - Classified as current if maturity or committed prepayment is within 12 months.
  - Loans grouped into risk pools with similar characteristics (LTV, property type, geography, vacancy, property condition).
  - Credit loss methodology: loss-rate approach incorporating expected loss severity and default probability.
    - Incorporates reasonable and supportable macroeconomic forecasts (e.g., GDP, employment), reverting to historical loss rates beyond the forecast horizon.
  - Interest income:
    - Potential problem/restructured loans: accrue interest if collectible and performing under terms.
    - Problem loans (e.g., >60 days delinquent, bankruptcy, foreclosure): recognize interest on a cash basis.
    - Cash received during foreclosure is treated as principal recovery.

nodes.title: Mortgage Loans
nodes.heading: 1.12 Mortgage Loans
nodes.start_phrase: Mortgage loan investments on the consolidated balance sheets are valued at the unpaid principal balance, net of an allowance for credit losses.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Accounting policies for investments, covering debt securities, equity securities, and mortgage loans.
- Debt securities:
  - Types include U.S. Treasury and agency securities, mortgage-backed securities, corporate and foreign bonds, and other debt securities.
  - Classified as current or long-term based on contractual maturities or intent to sell within 12 months; all classified as available-for-sale and carried at fair value (referenced Fair Value Note).
  - Impairment model:
    - If intent or requirement to sell before recovery: write down to fair value with loss in net income.
    - If no intent/requirement to sell: bifurcate impairment into credit-related (allowance for credit losses recognized in net income) and non-credit-related (recorded in OCI).
    - Credit assessment factors include severity of fair value decline, issuer/industry/geographic conditions, payment structure, missed payments, and rating changes.
    - Allowance limited to the amount fair value is below amortized cost; interest accrual suspended when collection is unlikely.
  - MBS/ABS income recognition uses effective yield based on anticipated prepayments; changes in prepayment estimates result in yield recalculation and catch-up adjustments to net income.
- Equity securities:
  - With readily available fair values are measured at fair value, with all changes recognized in net income.
- Mortgage loans:
  - Carried at unpaid principal balance net of an allowance for credit losses; classified as current if maturity or committed prepayment is within 12 months.
  - Loans are pooled by similar risk characteristics (e.g., LTV, property type, geography, vacancy, condition) for measuring expected credit losses.
  - Credit loss methodology uses a loss-rate approach reflecting loss severity and default probability; incorporates reasonable and supportable economic forecasts (e.g., GDP, employment) and reverts to historical loss rates thereafter.
  - Interest recognition: potential problem or restructured loans accrue interest if collectible and performing; problem loans (e.g., >60 days delinquent, in bankruptcy, in foreclosure) are on cash-basis; cash received during foreclosure is treated as principal return.

nodes.title: Other Investments
nodes.heading: 1.13 Other Investments
nodes.start_phrase: Other investments consist primarily of the following:
nodes.summary:
- Scope and accounting for “Other Investments”:
  - Private equity and hedge fund limited partnerships: accounted for under the equity method based on managers’ reported NAVs, typically on up to a three-month reporting lag; monitored quarterly for impairment, with any identified impairments recognized by reducing carrying value and charging net investment income.
  - Investment real estate: carried at depreciated cost (straight-line) including capital additions, net of other-than-temporary write-downs; assets held-for-sale measured at lower of carrying value or fair value less selling costs; fair value estimated using NOI capitalization and comparable sales; gains/losses at sale recognized as realized capital gains/losses.
  - Privately-placed equity securities: carried at cost less impairments with adjustments for observable price changes; required FHLB Boston membership shares are restricted and carried at cost.

- Net investment income (NII) and gains/losses recognition:
  - NII is recorded when earned.
  - Experience-rated products (large case pensions): investment performance (including realized and unrealized results) is credited directly to contract holders’ accounts and does not affect Company net income unless minimum guarantees are triggered. NII on assets supporting these products is recorded in NII and simultaneously passed through via a charge to benefit costs; related balances appear in policyholders’ funds.
  - Non-experience-rated investments: realized gains/losses included in NII; unrealized gains/losses recorded in accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI), net of tax.
  - Trade-date accounting for purchases/sales of debt/equity securities and alternative investments; closing-date accounting for mortgage loans and investment real estate.
  - For experience-rated products, both realized and unrealized gains/losses bypass the income statement and are credited to contract holders’ accounts (policyholders’ funds).

- Derivative financial instruments:
  - Used primarily for hedging interest rate, foreign exchange, and credit risks.
  - Instruments include interest rate swaps, treasury rate locks, forwards, futures, warrants, put options, and credit default swaps.

nodes.title: Net Investment Income
nodes.heading: 1.14 Net Investment Income
nodes.start_phrase: Net investment income on the Company’s investments is recorded when earned and is reflected in the Company’s net income (other than net investment income on assets supporting experience-rated products).
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Describes the company’s accounting and reporting for “Other investments,” net investment income, realized/unrealized gains and losses, and use of derivative financial instruments.
- Other investments:
  - Private equity and hedge fund limited partnerships accounted for under the equity method based on manager-provided valuations, typically reported with up to a three-month lag; investments reviewed at least quarterly for impairment, with impairments recognized through reductions in carrying value and charges to net investment income when identified.
  - Investment real estate carried at depreciated cost (straight-line), net of other-than-temporary write-downs; assets held-for-sale carried at lower of carrying value or fair value less selling costs; fair value estimated using NOI capitalization and comparable sales; gains/losses on sale recognized as realized capital gains/losses.
  - Privately placed equity securities carried at cost less impairments with adjustments for observable price changes; restricted FHLB Boston shares held at cost.
- Net investment income:
  - Recognized when earned; excludes the effect of assets supporting experience-rated products from impacting company net income unless minimum guarantees are triggered.
  - For large case pensions’ experience-rated products, investment results (including net investment income) are allocated to contract holders and reflected through benefit costs; balances reported in policyholders’ funds.
- Realized and unrealized gains/losses:
  - Non–experience-rated investments: realized gains/losses included in net investment income; specific identification method; trade-date accounting for securities/alternatives, closing-date for mortgage loans and real estate. Unrealized gains/losses recorded in accumulated other comprehensive income (net of tax).
  - Experience-rated investments: realized and unrealized gains/losses credited directly to contract holders’ accounts and reflected in policyholders’ funds, not in the company’s realized gains/losses or AOCI.
- Derivative financial instruments:
  - Used primarily for hedging interest rate, foreign exchange, and credit risks.
  - Instruments include interest rate swaps, treasury rate locks, forwards, futures, warrants, put options, and credit default swaps.

nodes.title: Derivative Financial Instruments
nodes.heading: 1.15 Derivative Financial Instruments
nodes.start_phrase: The Company uses derivative financial instruments in order to manage interest rate and foreign exchange risk and credit exposure.
nodes.summary:
- Describes “Other Investments” categories and accounting:
  - Private equity and hedge fund limited partnerships accounted for under the equity method; valuations based on fund manager reports (often audited) and typically reported on up to a three-month lag. Investments are monitored at least quarterly for impairment; known impairments are recognized via a carrying value reduction and charge to net investment income.
  - Investment real estate carried at depreciated cost (straight-line), including capital additions and net of other-than-temporary write-downs; held-for-sale assets at lower of carrying value or fair value less selling costs. Fair value estimated using NOI with capitalization rates and comparable sales. Gains/losses on sale recognized as realized capital gains/losses.
  - Privately placed equity securities at cost less impairments with adjustments for observable price changes. Required FHLBB shares are restricted and carried at cost.
- Explains net investment income recognition:
  - Recorded when earned and impacts net income except for assets supporting experience-rated products in large case pensions, where investment results are passed through daily to contract holders (subject to minimum guarantees).
  - For experience-rated products, investment income is included in net investment income and simultaneously credited to contract holders via benefit costs; balances shown in policyholders’ funds.
  - Realized gains/losses (non–experience-rated) flow through net investment income; specific identification used; trades for securities/alternatives on trade date; mortgages/real estate on closing date.
  - Realized gains/losses on experience-rated assets are credited directly to contract holders’ accounts (policyholders’ funds), not through realized gains/losses line.
  - Unrealized gains/losses (non–experience-rated) go to AOCI, net of tax; for experience-rated assets, unrealized amounts are credited directly to contract holders’ accounts (policyholders’ funds).
- Outlines derivative use:
  - Derivatives are used primarily for hedging interest rate, foreign exchange, and credit risks, including interest rate swaps, treasury rate locks, forwards, futures, warrants, put options, and credit default swaps.

nodes.title: Accounts Receivable
nodes.heading: 1.16 Accounts Receivable
nodes.start_phrase: Accounts receivable are stated net of allowances for credit losses, customer credit allowances, contractual allowances and estimated terminations.
nodes.summary:
- Accounts receivable: Presented net of allowances (credit losses, customer credit allowances, contractual allowances, estimated terminations). Detailed composition at December 31, 2022 and 2021: trade, vendor/manufacturer, premium, and other receivables totaling $27.503 billion (2022) and $24.431 billion (2021), including $227 million classified as assets held for sale in 2022. Allowance for credit losses was $333 million (2022) and $339 million (2021). Expected credit losses are estimated using historical data, current conditions, and reasonable forecasts; receivables generally settle in under 30 days.
- Inventories: Measured at the lower of cost or net realizable value using weighted average cost. Inventory control via regular store and LTC pharmacy physical counts and continuous cycle counts in distribution centers and mail facilities; accruals recorded for expected shrink based on historical trends and current results.
- Reinsurance recoverables: Reinsurance used to reduce required capital and support acquisitions/dispositions. Ceded reinsurance does not relieve primary liability. The company monitors reinsurer credit risk and concentrations; recoverables mainly from strongly rated third parties. Amounts recorded in other current assets or other assets; no material impact expected from unrecoverable reinsurance.
- Health care contract acquisition costs: Most insurance products are cancellable monthly; related costs generally expensed as incurred. For certain long-duration contracts, acquisition costs are deferred, recorded in other current assets or other assets, and amortized through operating expenses. Deferred acquisition costs were $1.2 billion (2022) and $895 million (2021), primarily Medicare Supplement commissions.
- Property and equipment: Carried at historical cost net of accumulated depreciation; depreciated on a straight-line basis over useful lives or lease terms, with useful lives generally ranging from 1 to 40 years (excerpt truncated).

nodes.title: Inventories
nodes.heading: 1.17 Inventories
nodes.start_phrase: Inventories are valued at the lower of cost or net realizable value using the weighted average cost method.
nodes.summary:
- Accounts receivable: Presented net of credit-related allowances (credit losses, customer and contractual allowances, estimated terminations). Composition at Dec 31:
  - 2022 (in millions): Trade $8,983; Vendor/manufacturer $12,395; Premium $2,676; Other $3,449; Total $27,503.
  - 2021 (in millions): Trade $7,932; Vendor/manufacturer $10,573; Premium $2,537; Other $3,389; Total $24,431.
  - Includes $227 million classified as assets held for sale at Dec 31, 2022. Allowance for credit losses was $333 million (2022) and $339 million (2021). Expected credit losses are estimated using historical data, current conditions, and reasonable, supportable forecasts; receivables are short-duration and typically settle in under 30 days.
- Inventories: Carried at lower of cost or net realizable value using weighted average cost. Physical counts performed regularly in retail stores and LTC pharmacies; distribution centers and mail facilities use cycle counts. The company accrues for anticipated physical inventory losses by location based on history and current trends.
- Reinsurance recoverables: Reinsurance used to reduce required capital and support acquisitions/dispositions; ceded agreements do not relieve the company of primary insurance liability. The company assesses reinsurer financial condition and concentration risks; does not expect unrecoverable reinsurance to be material. As of Dec 31, 2022, recoverables are primarily from well-rated third parties and are recorded in other current assets or other assets.
- Health care contract acquisition costs: Most insurance products are cancellable monthly; related acquisition costs are generally expensed as incurred. For certain long-duration contracts, costs are deferred, recorded in other current assets or other assets, and amortized over contract life; amortization is in operating expenses. Deferred acquisition costs were $1.2 billion (2022) and $895 million (2021), primarily Medicare Supplement commissions within the Health Care Benefits segment.
- Property and equipment: Recorded at historical cost, net of accumulated depreciation; depreciated on a straight-line basis over estimated useful lives or lease term, whichever is shorter. Useful lives generally range up to 40 years for buildings (section truncated).

nodes.title: Reinsurance Recoverables
nodes.heading: 1.18 Reinsurance Recoverables
nodes.start_phrase: The Company utilizes reinsurance agreements primarily to: (a) reduce required capital and (b) facilitate the acquisition or disposition of certain insurance contracts.
nodes.summary:
- Accounts Receivable: Reported net of credit, customer, contractual, and termination allowances. 2022 composition (in millions): Trade $8,983; Vendor/manufacturer $12,395; Premium $2,676; Other $3,449; Total $27,503 (vs. $24,431 in 2021). Includes $227 million classified as assets held for sale. Allowance for credit losses: $333 million (2022) vs. $339 million (2021). Loss estimates consider historical data, current conditions, and reasonable forecasts; receivables are short duration, typically settling in under 30 days.
- Inventories: Valued at lower of cost or net realizable value using weighted average cost. Inventory control via regular store/LTC physical counts and distribution/mail facility cycle counts, with interim accruals for expected shrink based on history and trends.
- Reinsurance Recoverables: Reinsurance used to reduce required capital and support acquisitions/dispositions; ceded reinsurance does not remove primary liability. Unrecoverable reinsurance not expected to be material. Company assesses reinsurers’ financial condition and concentration risk; recoverables primarily from highly rated third parties at 12/31/22. Recorded in other current assets or other assets.
- Health Care Contract Acquisition Costs: Most health products are cancelable monthly; acquisition costs for prepaid health care and indemnity are generally expensed. Certain long-duration insurance contract costs are deferred and amortized; deferred acquisition costs were $1.2 billion (2022) and $895 million (2021), mainly Medicare Supplement commissions, with amortization in operating expenses.
- Property and Equipment: Carried at historical cost less accumulated depreciation; straight-line depreciation over estimated useful lives or lease term if shorter. Useful lives generally range up to 1–40 years.

nodes.title: Health Care Contract Acquisition Costs
nodes.heading: 1.19 Health Care Contract Acquisition Costs
nodes.start_phrase: Insurance products included in the Health Care Benefits segment are cancellable by either the customer or the member monthly upon written notice.
nodes.summary:
- Accounts receivable are presented net of allowances for credit losses, customer credit allowances, contractual allowances, and estimated terminations. At December 31, 2022 vs. 2021 (in millions): Trade $8,983 vs. $7,932; Vendor and manufacturer $12,395 vs. $10,573; Premium $2,676 vs. $2,537; Other $3,449 vs. $3,389; Total $27,503 vs. $24,431. Includes $227 million classified as assets held for sale in 2022.
- Allowance for credit losses was $333 million (2022) and $339 million (2021). Expected credit losses are estimated using historical data, current conditions, and reasonable, supportable forecasts; receivables are short duration and typically settle in under 30 days.
- Inventories are carried at the lower of cost or net realizable value using weighted average cost. Physical counts occur regularly in retail stores and LTC pharmacies; distribution centers and mail facilities use continuous cycle counts. Interim accruals for inventory losses are based on historical results and current trends.
- Reinsurance recoverables arise from ceded reinsurance used to reduce required capital and support acquisitions/dispositions. Ceding does not release the Company from primary liability. Credit risk from reinsurers is monitored; exposures are largely to well-rated third parties as of year-end 2022. Recoverables are recorded in other current assets or other assets.
- Health care contract acquisition costs: Most insurance products are cancellable monthly; related acquisition costs are generally expensed as incurred. Certain long-duration contracts have deferred acquisition costs (DAC) recorded in other current assets or other assets and amortized over contract life; DAC was $1.2 billion (2022) and $895 million (2021), primarily Medicare Supplement commissions, with amortization included in operating expenses.
- Property and equipment are recorded at historical cost less accumulated depreciation, depreciated on a straight-line basis over estimated useful lives or lease term, generally with useful lives ranging from 1 to 40 years (buildings).

nodes.title: Property and Equipment
nodes.heading: 1.20 Property and Equipment
nodes.start_phrase: Property and equipment is reported at historical cost, net of accumulated depreciation.
nodes.summary:
- Accounts Receivable: Presented net of allowances (credit losses, customer credit, contractual allowances, estimated terminations). Composition at December 31: 2022/2021 (in millions) — Trade $8,983/$7,932; Vendor and manufacturer $12,395/$10,573; Premium $2,676/$2,537; Other $3,449/$3,389; Total $27,503/$24,431. Includes $227 million classified as assets held for sale at 12/31/22. Allowance for credit losses was $333 million (2022) and $339 million (2021). Expected credit losses are estimated using historical data, current conditions, and reasonable forecasts; receivables are short-duration, typically settling in under 30 days.

- Inventories: Stated at lower of cost or net realizable value using weighted average cost. Regular physical counts in retail stores and LTC pharmacies; cycle counts in distribution centers and mail facilities. Interim shrink accruals recorded by location based on history and current trends.

- Reinsurance Recoverables: Reinsurance used to reduce required capital and support acquisitions/dispositions. Ceded reinsurance does not release the Company from primary insurance liability. Company monitors reinsurer credit quality and concentration risk; recoverables primarily from well-rated third parties. Recorded in other current assets or other assets.

- Health Care Contract Acquisition Costs: Most acquisition costs for cancellable health contracts expensed as incurred; certain long-duration insurance contract costs deferred and amortized in operating expenses. Deferred acquisition costs were $1.2 billion (2022) and $895 million (2021), primarily commissions on Medicare Supplement products.

- Property and Equipment: Recorded at historical cost less accumulated depreciation; straight-line depreciation over estimated useful lives (generally 1–40 years for buildings/building and leasehold improvements; 3–10 years for fixtures, equipment, and internally developed software). Repairs expensed; major renewals capitalized; application development stage software costs capitalized. Balances (in millions) at 12/31: Total P&E $34,600 (2022)/$33,550 (2021); Accumulated depreciation and amortization $(21,483)/$(20,654); Net $13,117/$12,896. Includes $244 million classified as assets held for sale at 12/31/22. Depreciation expense: $2.4B (2022), $2.3B (2021), $2.1B (2020). 2021 included $261 million impairment tied to planned retail store closures.

- Right-of-Use Assets and Lease Liabilities: Identified at contract inception; recognized at commencement/renewal/significant remodel based on present value of future lease payments discounted using the Company’s incremental borrowing rate by asset class. Real estate lease renewal options generally not included as not reasonably certain; short-term leases (≤12 months) excluded from balance sheet with straight-line expense. For real estate, lease and nonlease components are combined; variable costs (e.g., taxes, CAM, insurance based on sales) expensed as incurred; fixed inclusive payments included in measurement.

- Goodwill: Business combinations accounted for using the acquisition method; goodwill recorded as the excess of purchase price over the fair value of net assets acquired and identifiable intangibles (section truncated).

nodes.title: Right-of-Use Assets and Lease Liabilities
nodes.heading: 1.21 Right-of-Use Assets and Lease Liabilities
nodes.start_phrase: The Company determines if an arrangement contains a lease at the inception of a contract.
nodes.summary:
- Property and equipment accounting: Repairs and maintenance expensed as incurred; major renewals/replacements capitalized and depreciated. Application development costs for significant internally developed software are capitalized and depreciated. Useful lives include 3–10 years for fixtures, equipment, and internally developed software; building/leasehold improvements are depreciated over their estimated lives.
- Property and equipment balances (in millions): At Dec 31, 2022 vs. 2021—Land: 1,996 vs. 2,038; Building and improvements: 4,545 vs. 4,225; Fixtures and equipment: 12,978 vs. 13,619; Leasehold improvements: 6,238 vs. 6,242; Software: 8,843 vs. 7,426; Total P&E: 34,600 vs. 33,550; Accumulated depreciation and amortization: (21,483) vs. (20,654); Net P&E: 13,117 vs. 12,896.
- Assets held for sale: Includes $244 million of property and equipment within assets held for sale at Dec 31, 2022 (see Note 2).
- Depreciation and impairment: Depreciation expense was $2.4B (2022), $2.3B (2021), $2.1B (2020). An impairment of $261M on property and equipment was recorded in 2021 related to planned retail store closures (see Note 6).
- Lease accounting (right-of-use assets and lease liabilities): Leases identified at contract inception; ROU assets and lease liabilities recognized at commencement/renewal/significant remodel based on present value of remaining lease payments using the Company’s incremental borrowing rate by asset class. ROU assets include prepaid amounts and are reduced by incentives. Real estate leases often have renewal options up to five years, generally not considered reasonably certain and therefore excluded from lease term; same approach for non-real estate leases. Short-term leases (12 months or less) are not recorded on the balance sheet; expense recognized straight-line.
- Lease components and costs: For real estate leases, lease and nonlease components are accounted for as a single component. Variable costs (e.g., percentage rent, taxes, CAM, insurance) are expensed as incurred. Fixed payments that include taxes/CAM/insurance are included in lease measurements. Additional lease details referenced in Note 6.
- Goodwill: Business combinations accounted for using the acquisition method; excess of purchase price over fair value of net assets and identifiable intangibles recorded as goodwill (policy introduction).

nodes.title: Goodwill
nodes.heading: 1.22 Goodwill
nodes.start_phrase: The Company accounts for business combinations using the acquisition method of accounting, which requires the excess cost of an acquisition over the fair value of net assets acquired and identifiable intangible assets to be recorded as goodwill.
nodes.summary:
- Property and equipment accounting: Repairs and maintenance expensed; major renewals/replacements capitalized and depreciated. Application development stage costs for significant internally developed software are capitalized. Useful lives include 3–10 years for fixtures, equipment, and internally developed software; building and leasehold improvements are depreciated over their estimated lives.
- Property and equipment balances (in millions): 2022 total $34,600 (land $1,996; buildings/improvements $4,545; fixtures/equipment $12,978; leasehold improvements $6,238; software $8,843); accumulated depreciation/amortization $(21,483); net $13,117. 2021 total $33,550; accumulated $(20,654); net $12,896. Includes $244 of assets held for sale at 12/31/22.
- Depreciation expense (includes finance/capital leases): $2.4B (2022), $2.3B (2021), $2.1B (2020). 2021 included a $261M impairment tied to planned retail store closures.
- Lease accounting (right-of-use assets and liabilities): Leases identified at inception; ROU assets and liabilities recognized at commencement, renewal, or significant remodel based on present value of remaining minimum payments. Uses incremental borrowing rate by asset class. Real estate lease renewals generally not considered reasonably certain; renewal options typically excluded from lease term for both real estate and non-real estate leases. Short-term leases (≤12 months) not recorded on balance sheet; expense recognized straight-line. For real estate leases, lease and nonlease components are combined; variable payments (e.g., taxes, CAM, insurance) expensed; fixed inclusive payments included in lease measurement.
- Goodwill: Recognized under acquisition method; not amortized; tested annually or when indicators arise using discounted cash flow and market multiple methods. No impairments in 2022 or 2020; in 2021 a $431M goodwill impairment was recorded for the LTC reporting unit.
- Intangible assets: Primarily trademarks/trade names, customer relationships, noncompetes, technology, provider networks, and VOBA, measured at acquisition-date fair value. Definite-lived intangibles amortized over estimated useful lives (generally straight-line; VOBA in proportion to estimated premiums). Indefinite-lived intangibles not amortized; tested annually for impairment.
- Recoverability of long-lived assets (excluding goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles): Tested when indicators arise at the lowest identifiable cash flow level; recoverability based on undiscounted cash flows; impairment measured using discounted cash flows. 2022: $117M office real estate optimization charges (abandonment of leased real estate, related ROU assets, and P&E) due to reduced corporate office space. 2021: ~$(1.4)B store impairment (ROU assets and P&E) tied to planned closure of ~900 retail stores (2022–2024). 2020: no material impairments.
- Indefinite-lived trademarks are valued for impairment testing using the relief-from-royalty method.

nodes.title: Intangible Assets
nodes.heading: 1.23 Intangible Assets
nodes.start_phrase: The Company’s identifiable intangible assets consist primarily of trademarks, trade names, customer contracts/relationships, covenants not to compete, technology, provider networks and value of business acquired (“VOBA”).
nodes.summary:
- Goodwill: Not amortized; tested for impairment annually or more frequently. Fair value of reporting units estimated using discounted cash flow and market multiple methods. Results: no goodwill impairments in 2022 and 2020; a $431 million impairment recorded in 2021 for the LTC reporting unit. See Note 5.

- Identifiable intangible assets: Primarily trademarks, trade names, customer relationships/contracts, non-compete agreements, technology, provider networks, and value of business acquired (VOBA). Initially measured at fair value at acquisition using valuation techniques and management estimates.

- Amortization: Definite-lived intangibles amortized over useful lives based on cash flow patterns; straight-line method except VOBA, which is amortized in proportion to estimated premiums over contract life. Indefinite-lived intangibles are not amortized; tested for impairment annually or when indicators arise. See Note 5.

- Recoverability of long-lived assets (excluding goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles): Tested when events/circumstances indicate potential non-recoverability. Assets grouped at the lowest level of identifiable cash flows. Step 1: compare carrying amount to undiscounted cash flows; if not recoverable, measure impairment by comparing carrying amount to discounted cash flows and record the excess as a loss.

- Impairment/optimization charges:
  - 2022: $117 million office real estate optimization related to abandonment of leased real estate, right-of-use (ROU) assets, and property/equipment due to flexible work arrangements.
  - 2021: Approximately $1.4 billion store impairment associated with planned closure of ~900 retail stores, impacting operating lease ROU assets and property/equipment.
  - 2020: No material long-lived asset impairments.
  - See Note 6 for lease-related charges.

- Indefinite-lived intangibles impairment: Fair value compared to carrying value; trademarks valued using the relief-from-royalty method.

- Cross-references: Note 5 “Goodwill and Other Intangibles” and Note 6 “Leases” for additional details.

nodes.title: Recoverability of Long-Lived Assets
nodes.heading: 1.24 Recoverability of Long-Lived Assets
nodes.start_phrase: The Company evaluates the recoverability of long-lived assets, excluding goodwill and indefinite-lived intangible assets, which are tested for impairment using separate tests described below, whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying value of such asset may not be recoverable.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines accounting policies for goodwill and identifiable intangible assets. Goodwill is not amortized and is tested annually (or more frequently) for impairment. Identifiable intangibles include trademarks, trade names, customer relationships/contracts, non-competes, technology, provider networks, and VOBA, measured at fair value at acquisition.
- Amortization: definite-lived intangibles are amortized over useful lives (straight-line for all except VOBA). VOBA is amortized in proportion to estimated premiums over the expected life of acquired contracts. Indefinite-lived intangibles are not amortized and are tested annually for impairment.
- Recoverability of long-lived assets (excluding goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles): impairment testing is triggered by indicators and performed at the lowest identifiable cash flow level. The process compares carrying value to undiscounted cash flows; if not recoverable, impairment is measured using discounted cash flows.
- Recorded impairment charges: 2022 office real estate optimization charges of $117 million from abandoning leased real estate/right-of-use assets and property/equipment; 2021 store impairment of approximately $1.4 billion related to planned closure of ~900 retail stores (2022–2024); no material long-lived asset impairments in 2020.
- Goodwill impairment testing uses a discounted cash flow and market multiple approach at the reporting unit level. No impairments in 2022 or 2020; in 2021, a $431 million goodwill impairment was recorded for the LTC reporting unit; no other reporting units impaired.
- Indefinite-lived intangible impairment testing applies the relief-from-royalty method; no impairments recognized in 2022, 2021, or 2020.
- Separate Accounts for large case pensions: assets and liabilities are at fair value, investment results accrue to contract holders who bear investment risk, assets are legally segregated, and related deposits/withdrawals/investment results are excluded from consolidated operations and cash flows; management fees are recognized as services revenue.
- Health care costs payable: includes unpaid medical/dental/pharmacy claims, capitation, risk-sharing amounts, and state assessments. IBNR covers incurred-but-not-reported claims, reported-but-unpaid claims, and certain post-period services the Company must cover.
- IBNR estimation relies on actuarial methods considering claim submission/processing patterns, medical cost trends, utilization, claim inventory, membership/product mix, and seasonality; methodology and assumptions were consistent in 2022.
- Completion factor approach: analyzes incurred-to-paid claim patterns by service month to estimate ultimate claim costs; most claims are paid within six months, though full resolution may take up to 48 months. For the most recent three months, estimates blend completion factors with assumed health care cost trend rates. Adjustments may be needed if submission/processing speeds differ from history.

nodes.title: Separate Accounts
nodes.heading: 1.25 Separate Accounts
nodes.start_phrase: Separate Accounts assets and liabilities related to large case pensions products represent funds maintained to meet specific objectives of contract holders who bear the investment risk.
nodes.summary:
- Describes the impairment testing approach for indefinite-lived intangible assets, including qualitative assessments and fair value measurements (market and income approaches), with no impairment losses recorded in 2020–2022.
- Explains Separate Accounts for large case pension products: assets and liabilities are carried at fair value, investment risk is borne by contract holders, assets are legally segregated, investment results bypass the consolidated statements, and management fees are recognized as services revenue over the period earned.
- Details the composition of health care costs payable, including unpaid medical/dental/pharmacy claims, IBNR, capitation costs, amounts due under provider risk-sharing arrangements, state assessments, and costs for services to be rendered post–balance sheet date when obligated.
- Outlines actuarial methods and key assumptions for estimating IBNR, emphasizing analysis of historical and projected claim submission/processing patterns (completion factors) and assumed health care cost trend rates; notes consistent application with no significant methodology changes in 2022.
- Describes the use of completion factors to estimate ultimate claim costs for older claims (generally >3 months), typical payment timing (most within six months, some up to 48+ months), and adjustments for claim inventory, processing speeds, trend, membership, and product mix.
- Notes sensitivity of reserves to faster or slower claim submission/processing and the blended use of completion factors and trend rates for less mature, recent claims (within three months of the reporting date).

nodes.title: Health Care Costs Payable
nodes.heading: 1.26 Health Care Costs Payable
nodes.start_phrase: Health care costs payable consist principally of unpaid fee-for-service medical, dental and pharmacy claims, capitation costs, other amounts due to providers pursuant to risk-sharing arrangements related to the Health Care Benefits segment’s Insured Commercial, Medicare and Medicaid products and accruals for state assessments.
nodes.summary:
- Indefinite-lived intangible assets: Tested for impairment using a relief-from-royalty income approach; no impairments recognized in 2020–2022.
- Separate Accounts (large case pensions): Assets and liabilities carried at fair value; investment results accrue directly to contract holders who bear investment risk; assets are legally segregated; related deposits/withdrawals and investment results excluded from consolidated operations and cash flows; management fees recognized as services revenue over the period earned.
- Health care costs payable: Comprised of unpaid medical/dental/pharmacy claims, IBNR (reported but unpaid and incurred but not reported), capitation, risk-sharing amounts, and state assessments; includes costs for services continuing after the reporting date when obligated. Estimates use actuarial principles with key assumptions of claim completion factors (from historical incurred-to-paid patterns) and the health care cost trend rate. 
  - Completion factors primarily used for claims incurred more than three months prior; for the most recent three months, a blend of completion factors and trend with greater weight on trend for the latest periods. Most claims pay within six months, but full resolution can take up to 48+ months.
  - Trend drivers include utilization, unit costs, product design, provider contracting, medical management, business mix, demographics, technology, prescription drug costs (including specialty), DTC pharma marketing, high-cost case clusters, claim intensity, regulation, and fraud.
  - Estimates involve significant judgment and are sensitive to completion factors and trend assumptions; quarterly re-evaluation may yield favorable or unfavorable development; no significant methodology or assumption changes in 2022; company records the actuarial best estimate but actual payments may differ and changes could be material. Reference to Note 7 for rollforward.
- Other insurance liabilities – unpaid claims: Primarily for short-duration group disability and term life; reserves include IBNR and are based on the present value of future benefits using assumed investment yields, mortality, morbidity, and expected Social Security recoveries. Certain LTD and life waiver liabilities are discounted (rates reflect expected investment returns or contractual terms). IBNR for life products estimated using completion factors with judgment; estimates can change with experience or yield shifts; no significant methodology changes in 2022. Balances at December 31: 2022—$243 million (other insurance liabilities) and $1.1 billion (other long-term insurance liabilities); 2021—$324 million and $1.3 billion, respectively.

nodes.title: Unpaid Claims
nodes.heading: 1.27 Unpaid Claims
nodes.start_phrase: Unpaid claims consist primarily of reserves associated with certain short-duration group disability and term life insurance contracts, including an estimate for IBNR as of the financial statement date.
nodes.summary:
- Estimation of health care costs payable relies on actuarial judgment, emphasizing recent incurred months, completion factors, and assumed health care cost trend rates that may be affected by seasonality, membership, and product mix.
- Health care cost trend is driven by utilization and unit cost changes, product design, provider contracting, medical management, business mix, demographics, technology, prescription drug costs (including specialty drugs), marketing, high-cost case clusters, claim intensity, regulation, and fraud.
- Estimates carry significant variability and are most uncertain for claims incurred within three months of the reporting date; results are highly sensitive to completion factors and trend assumptions.
- Each quarter, prior estimates are re-examined and may develop favorably or unfavorably; the company consistently records the actuarial best estimate and notes potential for material near-term changes.
- Unpaid claims (other insurance liabilities) primarily relate to short-duration group disability and term life contracts, including IBNR, and are based on assumptions for investment yields, mortality, morbidity, Social Security recoveries, incidence and recovery rates, and seasonality; certain liabilities are discounted.
- IBNR for life products is largely based on completion factors informed by historical patterns and operational indicators; no significant methodology changes in 2022.
- Reported unpaid claims balances at December 31, 2022: $243 million (other insurance liabilities) and $1.1 billion (other long-term insurance liabilities); at December 31, 2021: $324 million and $1.3 billion, respectively.
- Substantially all life and disability insurance liabilities are fully ceded via indemnity reinsurance, although the company remains directly obligated to policyholders.
- Future policy benefits include reserves for limited payment pension/annuity and long-term care; determined using actuarial principles (mortality, morbidity, retirement, expenses, interest rates). Assumed interest rates: 3.0%–11.3% (pension/annuity, 2022 and 2021) and 4.9%/5.1% (long-term care, 2022/2021).
- Future policy benefits balances at December 31, 2022: $385 million (current) and $5.0 billion (long-term); at December 31, 2021: $416 million and $5.1 billion, respectively.
- Premium deficiency reserve methodology is described; no reserve in 2022; a $16 million reserve existed in 2021 for Medicaid products in the Health Care Benefits segment.
- Policyholders’ funds comprise pension/annuity investment contracts and certain health customer funds; equal to deposits minus withdrawals/charges plus credited interest, net of experience-rated adjustments; interest rates 3.5%–4.8% in 2022 and 2021.
- HSA custodial funds formerly held (via PayFlex) were $2.9 billion at December 31, 2021 (restricted cash); none held at December 31, 2022 due to the PayFlex sale; classification guidance for current vs long-term liabilities is provided.
- Self-insurance liabilities cover general liability, workers’ compensation, auto, and health/medical; calculated using actuarial assumptions and historical experience; totaled $1.1 billion at both December 31, 2022 and 2021, recorded in accrued expenses and other long-term liabilities.

nodes.title: Future Policy Benefits
nodes.heading: 1.28 Future Policy Benefits
nodes.start_phrase: Future policy benefits consist primarily of reserves for limited payment pension and annuity contracts and long-term care insurance contracts.
nodes.summary:
- The company has ceded substantially all life and disability insurance liabilities to unrelated reinsurers via indemnity reinsurance, while remaining directly obligated to policyholders.
- Future policy benefits primarily cover reserves for limited-payment pension and annuity contracts and long-term care (LTC) insurance:
  - Reserves use actuarial assumptions for mortality, retirement, expenses, and interest, varying by plan, issue year, and duration.
  - Assumed interest rates for pension/annuity contracts: 3.0%–11.3% in both 2022 and 2021.
  - LTC assumed interest rate: 4.9% (2022) and 5.1% (2021); reserves reflect the present value of future benefits and maintenance costs less future gross premiums, based on mortality, morbidity, and interest assumptions.
  - As of Dec 31, 2022: $385 million in other insurance liabilities and $5.0 billion in other long-term insurance liabilities; as of Dec 31, 2021: $416 million and $5.1 billion, respectively.
- Premium deficiency reserves:
  - Recognized when expected future claims (including maintenance costs) exceed existing reserves plus anticipated future premiums and reinsurance recoveries; investment income is excluded for short-duration contracts.
  - No premium deficiency reserves at Dec 31, 2022; $16 million recorded at Dec 31, 2021 for Medicaid products in the Health Care Benefits segment.
- Policyholders’ funds:
  - Consist of reserves for pension and annuity investment contracts and customer funds for certain health contracts; calculated as deposits less withdrawals/charges plus credited interest, net of experience-rated adjustments.
  - Credited rates for pension/annuity investment contracts: 3.5%–4.8% in 2022 and 2021.
  - Company previously held HSA funds (restricted cash) for members prior to the June 2022 PayFlex sale; none at Dec 31, 2022; approximately $2.9 billion at Dec 31, 2021 with corresponding liability in policyholders’ funds.
  - Classified as current or long-term based on expected payment timing.
- Self-insurance liabilities:
  - The company self-insures certain general liability, workers’ compensation, auto liability, and health/medical risks, with third-party coverage to limit exposure.
  - Accruals include reported and IBNR claims, based on standard actuarial assumptions and historical experience.
  - Totaled $1.1 billion at both Dec 31, 2022 and Dec 31, 2021, recorded in accrued expenses and other long-term liabilities.

nodes.title: Premium Deficiency Reserves
nodes.heading: 1.29 Premium Deficiency Reserves
nodes.start_phrase: The Company evaluates its insurance contracts to determine if it is probable that a loss will be incurred.
nodes.summary:
- Reinsurance: Substantially all life and disability insurance liabilities are fully ceded to unrelated third parties via indemnity reinsurance, but the Company remains directly obligated to policyholders.
- Future policy benefits: Primarily reserves for limited-payment pension/annuity and long-term care contracts. Assumptions include mortality, retirement, expense, and interest; interest rates on pension/annuity reserves ranged from 3.0% to 11.3% in 2022 and 2021. Long-term care reserves use mortality, morbidity, and interest assumptions with assumed rates of 4.9% (2022) and 5.1% (2021). Balances recorded: $385 million (other insurance liabilities) and $5.0 billion (other long-term insurance liabilities) at 12/31/22; $416 million and $5.1 billion, respectively, at 12/31/21.
- Premium deficiency reserves: The Company recognizes a reserve when expected future claims and maintenance costs exceed existing reserves plus future premiums and reinsurance recoveries (investment income excluded for short-duration contracts). No premium deficiency reserves at 12/31/22; $16 million recorded at 12/31/21 for Medicaid products in the Health Care Benefits segment.
- Policyholders’ funds: Reserves for pension/annuity investment contracts and certain health customer funds equal deposits less withdrawals/charges plus credited interest (3.5%–4.8% in 2022 and 2021) and reflect experience-rating rights. The Company held HSA funds prior to the June 2022 PayFlex sale; none at 12/31/22. HSA balance was approximately $2.9 billion at 12/31/21 (other current assets with a corresponding policyholders’ funds liability; treated as restricted cash). Liabilities are classified as current or other long-term based on expected payment timing.
- Self-insurance liabilities: The Company self-insures certain general liability, workers’ compensation, auto liability, and health/medical risks, with third-party coverage to limit exposure. Accruals are based on actuarial assumptions and historical claims. Total self-insurance liabilities were $1.1 billion at both 12/31/22 and 12/31/21, recorded in accrued expenses and other long-term liabilities.

nodes.title: Policyholders’ Funds
nodes.heading: 1.30 Policyholders’ Funds
