nodes.title: CMS Actions
nodes.heading: 16.5.6 CMS Actions
nodes.start_phrase: CMS regularly audits the Company’s performance to determine its compliance with CMS’s regulations and its contracts with CMS and to assess the quality of services it provides to Medicare beneficiaries.
nodes.summary:
- Ongoing litigation and regulatory scrutiny over out-of-network benefit payment and administration practices, including subpoenas and investigations by state Attorneys General and other regulators, with the possibility of additional actions; similar litigation has affected other major health insurers.
- CMS oversight: routine audits of Medicare plan compliance and quality; reliance on provider-submitted diagnosis coding that drives risk-adjusted premium payments; continuing audits by CMS and HHS-OIG focused on validation of diagnosis coding and medical record support.
- Evolution of RADV audit methodology:
  - 2012 notice for contract year 2011 forward introduced extrapolation and contemplated an FFS Adjuster; pre-2011 audits did not extrapolate or apply the adjuster.
  - Proposed 2018 methodology targeted certain high-risk conditions and high-diagnosis members, used extrapolation, and omitted the FFS Adjuster; CMS began contract-level audits for 2014–2015 under this approach before finalization.
  - Final RADV Audit Rule (Jan 30, 2023) authorizes extrapolation for payment years 2018 forward for both RADV and OIG audits, eliminates the FFS Adjuster, and prioritizes contracts at highest risk of overpayment based on statistical modeling (e.g., coding intensity, prior unsupported diagnoses).
- Uncertainty around future CMS/OIG audit selections, potential retroactive refunds (including pre-2018), prospective premium adjustments, and impacts on bid assumptions and actuarial soundness; potential premium/fee refunds from RADV, Public Exchange, OIG, and MLR-related audits could be material and adversely affect results, cash flows, and financial condition.
- Clarification that the RADV Audit Rule does not apply to CMS Part C Improper Payment Measures audits or HHS-RADV programs.
- Civil Investigative Demands (CIDs) from DOJ Civil Division regarding patient chart reviews and risk adjustment data submissions under Medicare Parts C and D; company is cooperating.
- Separate 2017 CID from SDNY concerning potential false Medicare Part D prescription drug claims; company is cooperating.
- Stockholder litigation: multiple securities class actions and a derivative action alleging omissions/misstatements about the LTC business unit; one key federal case dismissed with prejudice and affirmed on appeal; related cases stayed or amended with motions to dismiss pending.
- ERISA class actions (Radcliffe and Flaim) alleging fiduciary breaches/prohibited transactions tied to Aetna 401(k) Plan investments in company stock during 2017–2019; consolidated case dismissed with prejudice, now on appeal to the Second Circuit; related ERISA document request addressed.
- Demand to inspect books and records under Delaware Section 220 related to potential board fiduciary breaches concerning opioids.
- Additional ongoing legal and regulatory matters across a broad range of issues: bad faith, malpractice, fiduciary duty, claims processing and payment, pharmacy dispensing, regulatory compliance, marketing practices, provider network design and terminations, coverage rescission, privacy/data use, antitrust, contracts, product liability, intellectual property, and employment.

- Government investigations (Medicare/Medicaid): Civil Investigative Demands from the DOJ regarding patient chart reviews and risk adjustment data submissions under Medicare Parts C and D; a separate CID from SDNY about potential false Medicare Part D claims; the Company is cooperating and producing documents.
- Stockholder litigation: Multiple securities class and derivative actions alleging omissions/misrepresentations tied to the performance of the Company’s LTC business unit; one key federal case was dismissed with prejudice and affirmed on appeal; related actions were stayed, with amended complaints filed and dismissal motions pending.
- ERISA litigation: Two class actions (Radcliffe and Flaim) alleging fiduciary breaches and prohibited transactions concerning Aetna 401(k) Plan investments in company stock tied to LTC-related losses; cases consolidated and ultimately dismissed with prejudice; plaintiffs have appealed; the Company responded to an ERISA §104(b) document request.
- Books-and-records demand: A Delaware Section 220 demand seeking inspection related to potential fiduciary breaches by the Board concerning opioids.
- Other legal/regulatory matters: The Company faces additional proceedings, investigations, and audits (with CIDs/subpoenas) spanning alleged bad faith, malpractice, fiduciary breaches, claims handling, dispensing practices, regulatory non-compliance, marketing misconduct, benefit denials, provider network issues, rescissions, privacy concerns, anticompetitive conduct, contract disputes, product liability, IP, and employment matters; the Company is cooperating with authorities.

nodes.title: Stockholder Matters
nodes.heading: 16.5.8 Stockholder Matters
nodes.start_phrase: Beginning in February 2019, multiple class action complaints, as well as a derivative complaint, were filed by putative plaintiffs against the Company and certain current and former officers and directors.
nodes.summary:
- Regulatory audits and potential financial impacts: Possible material premium or fee refunds/adjustments arising from CMS, OIG, RADV, and Public Exchange-related audits, including MLR reviews; note that the RADV Audit Rule does not apply to CMS Part C Improper Payment Measures audits or HHS-RADV programs.
- Medicare and Medicaid CIDs: DOJ Civil Investigative Demands concerning patient chart reviews and risk adjustment data submissions for Medicare Parts C and D; a separate 2017 SDNY CID regarding potential false Medicare Part D drug reimbursement claims; the Company is cooperating.
- Stockholder litigation: Multiple securities class action and derivative suits alleging omissions/misrepresentations tied to the performance of the Company’s LTC business; several cases consolidated; a key federal case dismissed with prejudice and affirmed on appeal; other related cases stayed, then amended, with motions to dismiss filed.
- ERISA class actions: Two suits (Radcliffe and Flaim) against CVS Health, Aetna, and certain individuals alleging fiduciary breaches and prohibited transactions involving Aetna 401(k) Plan investments in company stock during 2017–2019; cases consolidated and ultimately dismissed with prejudice; plaintiffs have appealed; the Company responded to a related ERISA §104(b) document request.
- Books and records demand: A Delaware Section 220 demand seeking inspection related to potential Board fiduciary breaches concerning opioid matters.
- Other legal and regulatory proceedings: Ongoing litigation, investigations, and audits across numerous areas, including bad faith, malpractice, fiduciary duty, claims processing, medication dispensing, regulatory compliance, marketing practices, claims payment administration, provider network issues, rescissions, privacy, anticompetitive conduct, contracts, product liability, intellectual property, and employment; the Company is responding to CIDs, subpoenas, and similar government requests.

nodes.title: Other Legal and Regulatory Proceedings
nodes.heading: 16.5.9 Other Legal and Regulatory Proceedings
nodes.start_phrase: The Company is also a party to other legal proceedings and is subject to government investigations, inquiries and audits and has received and is cooperating with the government in response to CIDs, subpoenas, or similar process from various governmental agencies requesting information.
nodes.summary:
- Regulatory audits and refunds: The company warns that premium or fee refunds/adjustments from regulatory audits (including RADV, Public Exchange, CMS, OIG, and MLR rebate audits) could be material and adversely affect results, cash flows, and financial condition. The RADV Audit Rule does not apply to CMS Part C Improper Payment Measures or HHS-RADV programs.
- DOJ and SDNY CIDs: The company received Civil Investigative Demands from the DOJ regarding patient chart reviews tied to Medicare Parts C and D risk adjustment submissions and from SDNY concerning potential false Medicare Part D claims; it is cooperating and providing information.
- Securities and derivative litigation: Multiple class and derivative actions allege omissions/misrepresentations about the performance of the company’s Long-Term Care (LTC) business. One federal case was dismissed with prejudice and affirmed on appeal; other related cases were stayed, amended, and are subject to motions to dismiss.
- ERISA litigation: Two class actions (Radcliffe and Flaim) allege fiduciary breaches and prohibited transactions related to Aetna 401(k) Plan investments in company stock tied to LTC performance. The consolidated case was dismissed with prejudice; plaintiffs appealed. A related ERISA document request was answered.
- Books and records demand: A Delaware Section 220 demand seeks inspection related to potential board fiduciary breaches concerning opioids.
- Other legal/regulatory proceedings: The company faces a wide range of claims and government actions (some class/derivative), including bad faith, malpractice, fiduciary breaches, claims processing, dispensing of medications, regulatory compliance, marketing, payment/administration of benefits, provider network structure and terminations, rescissions, privacy, anticompetitive conduct, contract disputes, product liability, IP, and employment matters.
- Government contract risks: Awards—especially Medicaid and other government contracts in Health Care Benefits—are frequently protested, which can reverse, delay, or modify awards; the company will defend its awards.
- Heightened industry scrutiny: Regulators and legislators are increasing review and litigation over premium rates, utilization management, medical policies, complaints/appeals, privacy, network adequacy and performance-based networks, provider terminations, directory accuracy, MLR calculations/rebates, delegated arrangements, rescissions, limited/student health products, PBM practices (rebates, pricing, narrow networks, formulary tiers), sales/customer service, vendor oversight, and claim payments (including out-of-network).
- Potential sanctions and impacts: Government actions may delay premium increases and result in business restrictions, practice changes, retroactive premium adjustments, refunds, withheld payments, damages, fines/penalties, and sanctions up to licensure suspension or exclusion from government programs.
- Forward-looking risk statement: The company cannot assure that operations, financial condition, or cash flows will avoid material adverse effects from new or interpreted laws/regulations, investigations, audits or enforcement, qui tam developments, or other legal proceedings.
- Segment reporting: The company has three operating segments—Health Care Benefits, Pharmacy Services, and Retail/LTC—and a Corporate/Other segment. The CODM evaluates segments using adjusted operating income (excluding amortization of intangibles and other non-ordinary items). Non-GAAP measures are used for performance analysis but are not GAAP substitutes.
- Government revenue exposure: Federal government revenue comprised 18% (2022), 17% (2021), and 16% (2020) of total revenues, primarily from CMS contracts covering Medicare-eligible individuals in the Health Care Benefits segment.

nodes.title: Segment Reporting
nodes.heading: 17.Segment Reporting
nodes.start_phrase: The Company has three operating segments, Health Care Benefits, Pharmacy Services and Retail/LTC, as well as a Corporate/Other segment.
nodes.summary:
- Ongoing legal matters include class actions and derivative claims; the company is defending these cases.
- Government contract awards, especially Medicaid and other public-sector health contracts, are frequently protested, which can reverse, delay, or modify awards and adversely affect results.
- Heightened regulatory reviews, audits, and litigation across many health care business practices (e.g., premium rates, utilization management, medical policies, appeals, privacy, network adequacy and directories, MLR/rebates, delegated arrangements, rescissions, limited-benefit/student plans, PBM practices, sales and customer service, vendor oversight, and claims payments) continue industry-wide.
- Potential consequences of government actions include delayed rate increases, business restrictions, practice changes, retroactive premium adjustments, refunds, withheld premiums, damages, fines, penalties, sanctions, licensure suspension/loss, and exclusion from government programs.
- The company cautions that future laws/regulations, interpretations of existing rules, investigations, audits/enforcement, qui tam litigation, and other legal proceedings could materially affect its business, results, and cash flows or require changes in business practices.
- Segment reporting: three operating segments (Health Care Benefits, Pharmacy Services, Retail/LTC) plus Corporate/Other; performance evaluated by the CODM using non-GAAP adjusted operating income (operating income excluding amortization of intangibles and certain non-core items).
- 2020–2022 segment data presented, including external and intersegment revenues, net investment income, adjusted operating income, and D&A; federal government revenues were 16%–18% of consolidated revenues, largely from CMS Medicare contracts within Health Care Benefits.
- Notes clarify intersegment eliminations and that Pharmacy Services revenues include significant retail co-payments; Maintenance Choice arrangements can create intersegment adjusted operating income eliminations.
- Reconciliation from GAAP operating income to adjusted operating income for 2020–2022 provided; 2022 adjustments include intangible amortization, office real estate optimization, gains on divestitures (bswift, PayFlex), opioid litigation charges, and losses on assets held for sale (notably LTC).
- Additional adjustment explanations cover prior years: Aetna integration costs (2020–2021), retail store impairments and LTC goodwill impairment (2021), purchase price adjustment (2021), ACA risk corridor receipt and gain on Workers’ Compensation divestiture (2020); rationale for excluding intangible amortization from non-GAAP metrics is detailed.
- Independent auditor (Ernst & Young LLP) issued an unqualified opinion on internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) as of December 31, 2022, based on COSO 2013, and an unqualified opinion on the 2020–2022 consolidated financial statements.
- Critical Audit Matter: valuation of health care costs payable (IBNR); significant judgment around completion factors and trend assumptions; auditors tested controls, data completeness/accuracy, methodologies and assumptions, and developed an independent reserve range.
- Item 9 disclosures: no changes or disagreements with accountants; disclosure controls and procedures deemed effective by CEO/CFO; management concluded ICFR is effective per COSO; no material changes in ICFR in Q4 2022; no other reportable information.

structure.summary:
- Signatures: The Form 10-K is executed on February 8, 2023 by CVS Health Corporation. Principal signatories include Shawn M. Guertin (Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, Principal Financial Officer), Karen S. Lynch (President and Chief Executive Officer, Principal Executive Officer and Director), James D. Clark (Senior Vice President – Controller and Chief Accounting Officer, Principal Accounting Officer), the Chair of the Board Roger N. Farah, and multiple directors (including Fernando Aguirre, Jeffrey R. Balser, C. David Brown II, Alecia A. DeCoudreaux, Nancy-Ann M. DeParle, Anne M. Finucane, Edward J. Ludwig, Jean-Pierre Millon, Mary L. Schapiro, William C. Weldon).

- Exhibit 4.21 – Description of Common Stock:
  - Authorized capital as of February 8, 2023: 3,200,000,000 common shares (par $0.01), 120,619 cumulative preferred shares (par $0.01), and 50,000,000 preference shares (par $1.00).
  - Common stock rights: one vote per share; no cumulative voting; majority vote standard in uncontested director elections and plurality in contested elections; dividends and liquidation rights subordinate to any designated preferences of preferred and preference stock; no preemptive rights.
  - Amendments: Charter and By-Laws amendable under Delaware law—board approval required for Charter changes; stockholder approval generally by majority of votes cast; By-Laws may be amended by stockholders (majority of outstanding) or by a majority of directors at a meeting with quorum.
  - Anti-takeover features: Board authority to issue preferred and preference stock with customizable terms; board authority to create and manage rights to purchase securities (including adoption, redemption, amendment of any rights plan); written consent by stockholders permitted only if initiated per Charter/By-Laws with a record date request by holders of at least 25% of voting power; fundamental transactions require board approval and majority stockholder vote; business combinations with 10%+ related persons require approval by a majority of disinterested shares unless approved by continuing directors or fair price provisions are met; CVS Health is subject to DGCL Section 203 restrictions on business combinations with interested stockholders.

- Exhibit 21.1 – Subsidiaries of CVS Health Corporation (as of December 31, 2022):
  - Broad enterprise structure spanning retail pharmacy (CVS Pharmacy, Inc. and state-specific LLCs), pharmacy benefit management and specialty pharmacy (Caremark entities, specialty/mail pharmacies across multiple states, Red Oak Sourcing, Wellpartner), home infusion (Coram and related entities), long-term care pharmacy (Omnicare and numerous affiliated LLCs and acquisitions), retail clinics (MinuteClinic entities in many states), distribution and logistics entities, sourcing and media/exchange services.
  - Insurance and health plan operations under Aetna Inc.: extensive network of health insurance, HMO, Medicaid/Medicare, dental, and administrative subsidiaries across numerous U.S. states (e.g., Aetna Health Inc. entities; Coventry-branded companies; Aetna Better Health plans) and multiple insurance carriers (Aetna Life Insurance Company, First Health Life & Health Insurance Company, Continental Life Insurance Company of Brentwood, Tennessee, American Continental Insurance Company, Silverscript Insurance Company, Accendo Insurance Company).
  - Joint ventures and partnerships with health systems (e.g., Innovation Health, Texas Health + Aetna, Banner Health and Aetna, Sutter Health and Aetna, Allina Health and Aetna).
  - International operations through Aetna International and related entities in the UK, Ireland, Bermuda, Hong Kong, Singapore, China, India, Indonesia, UAE, and other jurisdictions; includes reinsurance/captive and financial management entities.
  - Ownership notes for select entities (e.g., Coram Clinical Trials, CVS Cabot/Shaw Holdings, Omnicare) and clarification that omitted subsidiaries are not insurance companies and are not “significant subsidiaries” under Regulation S-X Rule 1-02(w).

- Exhibit 23.1 – Auditor Consent: Ernst & Young LLP consents to incorporation by reference of its February 8, 2023 reports on the consolidated financial statements and on internal control over financial reporting into CVS Health’s automatic shelf registration on Form S-3ASR (No. 333-238506) and multiple Form S-8 registrations.

- Exhibits 31.1 and 31.2 – Section 302 Certifications: CEO (Karen S. Lynch) and CFO (Shawn M. Guertin) certify they have reviewed the 10-K; that it fairly presents the company’s financial condition, results, and cash flows; describe responsibility for and design/evaluation of disclosure controls and procedures and internal control over financial reporting; disclose any material changes to ICFR; and confirm disclosure to auditors and the audit committee of any significant deficiencies, material weaknesses, or fraud.

- Exhibits 32.1 and 32.2 – Section 906 Certifications: CEO and CFO certify, for purposes of 18 U.S.C. § 1350 and Exchange Act Rules 13a-14(b)/15d-14(b), that the 10-K complies with Section 13(a) or 15(d) of the Exchange Act and fairly presents, in all material respects, the financial condition and results of operations of the Company.
